title: Atlas of Questions
ending: The archive keeper closes the atlas, leaving room for corrections. “The lost neighborhood and the shared night sky are both here, with the claims we could support and the questions we could not settle. It is ready for its next reader—not because our answers are final, but because someone else can examine them.”

steps.message: Field note. The notebook records where, when and how the observation was made. In this teaching case, two pots seem to dry at different rates; a memory of 'the drier one' would lose important context.
Calibrated scale. A known reference exposes an offset in the scale. Calibration ties readings to a standard; it does not remove every source of error.

Controlled comparison. The teaching comparison changes light while holding pot size and starting water fixed. Controlling these conditions narrows the explanations; it does not guarantee all confounders vanished.
Hypothesis. The observed difference and the explicit light-exposure question suggest the same hypothesis as the longer note-and-pattern route. This is a candidate explanation, not proof.
Testable question. If the proposed explanation matters, otherwise similar pots under different light should lose different amounts of water. That prediction makes a possible failure visible.
Measurement series. Repeated readings reveal small fluctuations that a single reading would hide. Keep the variation rather than choosing the most pleasing number.
Measurement record. The record pairs each reading with its conditions. Another observer can now ask whether the difference is larger than the measurement uncertainty.
Experimental protocol. The written protocol says what will be compared, measured and recorded. It turns a private trick into a procedure another person can attempt.

Repeatable experiment. The arrangement can be repeated from the record. A later attempt may disagree: repeatability is an opportunity to test the result, not a promise of agreement. “Our first reader has a question and a way to test it,” says the archive keeper. “Keep that standard as we visit the other collections. The pots can stay here.”

Argument. The levy argument connects an equal ten-coin charge to equal burden. The connection is now explicit enough to challenge without changing the subject.
Counterexample. Mira loses50% of her monthly money; Daro loses5%. Under a proportional-burden meaning, the equal-burden premise fails—even though the argument's conditional form was valid.
Explicit premises. Premise1: equal payments imply equal burdens. Premise2: each household pays ten coins. Conclusion: each household bears equal burden. The first premise is doing the disputed work.

Valid argument. Given those two levy premises, the conclusion follows in this supplied conditional form. But valid form cannot rescue a false premise: equal coin amounts may not mean equal burdens. Debate host: ‘We have not chosen a tax. We have learned why a sound inference can carry an unsound premise. Now the library needs that same care with words.’

Collation. A says ‘opened’; B says ‘barred’; damaged C preserves a gap. The disagreement concerns an action with opposite consequences, not merely spelling.

Annotated translation. No coins changed hands, and a child slept safely nearby. ‘Kept the person in their care’ best fits this invented context; the note records why ‘fee’ was rejected rather than pretending the dictionary had one answer.
Variant table. Under the lemma ‘At dusk, the keeper…’, the alternatives remain side by side. A reader can see both the difference and the evidence used to discuss it.

Textual family. The shared doubled word suggests copying or a common source. But B consulted another copy: this modern curator's tentative family diagram must allow borrowing, not pretend every text has one clean parent.

Reconstructed reading. C's ‘They waited outside until morning’ makes ‘barred’ a plausible restoration. A's contrary reading still exists, so the supplied word is a reasoned conjecture, not recovered certainty.
Critical text. The edited passage reads ‘At dusk, the keeper [barred?] the gate for the travelers.’ Brackets and a question mark prevent the restoration from posing as untouched evidence.
Critical edition. The edition prints the tentative reading and retains ‘opened’ from A in its notes. Another editor can disagree without losing sight of the surviving witnesses.

Parallel edition. The passage, alternatives and contextual translation are visible together. Readers can retrace why ‘barred’ remains tentative while the child—not a fee—is the better-supported sense of ‘charge’. Editor: ‘We have not made disagreement disappear. We have made the readings and our choices inspectable. The next collection asks whether an unknown number can be handled with the same openness.’

Numeral. The position of a digit changes its value: in a decimal notation, 3 in 30 is not 3 in 3. This modern demonstration makes place value explicit; it is not an exclusive origin claim.
Equation. A workshop problem becomes x + 5 = 12: the unknown is represented without guessing its value. The equality states a constraint, not a magic answer.
Completing the square. For x² + 6x, adding a square of area9 completes the larger square (x + 3)². The geometry explains why a correction term must be added, not merely memorized.
Written calculation. The written calculation keeps intermediate quantities outside the calculator's memory. Another person can retrace the arithmetic and locate an error.
Equivalent equation. Subtracting 5 from both sides preserves this equality, leaving x = 7. Applying an operation on only one side would change the problem.
Ledger. Transactions are recorded as amounts owed and received. A running account reveals an unpaid balance that isolated receipts can conceal.
Solved equation. The value 7 satisfies the original equation when substituted back. This recipe solves the supplied linear case, not every possible equation by one inverse operation.
Balanced ledger. The example's opposing entries reconcile to the same total. This is a balanced account, not proof that every transaction was legitimate.
General solution. The same reasoning gives x = b − a for x + a = b. One worked transaction has become a reusable method.

Quadratic method. Completing the square turns a quadratic into a form from which candidate roots can be checked. The algebraic method extends the geometric example; domain and sign conditions still matter. Mathematics teacher: “The entries balance, and the method reaches beyond this one bargain. Keep checking the roots against the original problem; a tidy account alone cannot tell us whether a bargain is fair.”

Light ray. A ray represents a possible path of light, not a physical thread. Moving the source changes which paths reach the screen.
Placed.
Inverted image. In the dark room, rays from the top and bottom of the scene cross at the aperture and make an inverted image. Stray light would make that image harder to see.
Camera obscura. An enclosure and small opening make a portable camera obscura. This teaching construction turns a room-sized optical effect into a usable reference tool.
Refraction model. At a boundary between materials, light can change direction. The simplified ray model predicts a bent path; it omits the full angle-dependent calculation.
Focused image. A suitably arranged lens brings rays from a scene point toward a corresponding image point. Moving the screen away from that position blurs the image.
Optical experiment. The aperture, source and screen can be varied and the observations repeated. The resulting evidence bears on an account of vision, not on every aspect of human perception at once.

Image-forming model. The model connects scene points, light paths and image points. It explains the inversion without needing a picture to travel intact through the hole. Optics curator: “The little aperture turns the scene upside down, just as our model predicts. Now we can change the apparatus and see where the explanation holds.”

Projection construction. In this modern teaching reconstruction, the optical model supplies a chosen viewpoint and picture plane. It does not claim that Renaissance perspective historically required a camera obscura.
Paint. Pigment supplies color and a binder holds it to the surface. Different combinations permit different marks; paint is not simply colored light.
Occlusion study. A foreground column hides part of the wall behind it. Occlusion supplies a depth cue without requiring the viewer to calculate a vanishing point.
Vanishing point. A family of parallel lines receding from the picture plane converges toward one vanishing point in this construction. Different directions need not share that point.
Perspective grid. The horizon and vanishing point organize a grid of receding space. The grid is a particular viewing convention, not a ranking of artistic traditions.
Perspective drawing. The courtyard plan is projected from one selected viewpoint. Change that viewpoint and a different drawing can be equally coherent.
Scaled architectural view. Measured proportions connect the image to the courtyard plan. The view is now checkable, while still omitting parts hidden from its chosen observer.
Spatial painting. Paint can turn the prepared perspective drawing into a spatial painting directly. A separate tonal study may help, but is not a compulsory intermediate object.

Courtyard painting. The courtyard has a coherent spatial reading assembled from projection, tone and overlap. The achievement is one convincing image, not a universal solution to painting. Workshop apprentice: “The courtyard finally has depth, and its proportions can be checked against the plan. This viewpoint makes a convincing picture; it need not be the only way to paint.”

Anatomy record. The teaching record distinguishes the adult human lower jaw from the inherited two-part account. Age and specimen identity are recorded: adult fusion cannot be generalized to every developmental stage.
Anatomical plate. The drawing makes the observed jaw contour inspectable away from the specimen. A plate is an argument made visible, and can introduce its own distortions.
Anatomical discrepancy. The inherited two-part lower-jaw account and the adult human observation do not match. This specific discrepancy is more useful than declaring all older medicine mistaken.
Labeled anatomy. Labels connect claims to particular structures instead of to an undifferentiated picture. Readers can now point to exactly where an account disagrees.
Comparative anatomy. Comparing species and specimen ages asks whether an animal-based account was transferred too broadly. A difference must be located before it can support a correction.
Anatomical atlas. The plates are organized for comparison. An atlas makes repeated inspection possible; its authority still depends on the observations and drawing choices behind it.

Supported correction. Repeated adult-human observations support the correction in this bounded case. The historical research contrasts Vesalius's earlier Tabulae with the Fabrica; his own account changed too.

Annotated correction. The note identifies the claim, observations and remaining limits. Correcting the jaw account does not erase Vesalius's continuing debts to Galen or certify every claim in the atlas. Anatomy curator: “The jaw will not conform to the inherited drawing. Our correction now shows its evidence, without pretending every other page in the atlas is beyond question.”

Flow estimate. This illustrative modern calculation uses a heart rate of60 beats/minute and a stroke-volume estimate of50mL/beat: flow is3L/minute. These are teaching numbers, not a quotation of Harvey's estimates.
One-way valve model. The supplied vein observations show flow favored in one direction. A valve can constrain movement without itself being the pump.
Capillary evidence. Malpighi's later microscopic observations, reported in1661, showed fine connections in frog tissue. These are not observations made by Harvey himself.
Throughput estimate. At the illustrative flow of3L/minute, ten minutes gives30L passing through. Keeping units visible prevents multiplying a heartbeat count by time twice.
Directional vessel map. The vessel diagram records those directions rather than merely drawing connected tubes. It narrows which possible circulation routes fit the observations.

Quantity contradiction. Thirty liters passing through in ten minutes greatly exceeds an illustrative5L blood volume. A simple one-pass consumption account would require implausibly rapid replacement; recirculation is a candidate explanation.
Circulation model. The heart and directed vessels form a candidate circuit. The diagram predicts a return route; drawing it is not yet observing every connection.

Recirculation argument. The circuit explains how a large throughput can coexist with a much smaller standing blood volume. This is one part of Harvey's reasoning, not a replacement for his other arguments.

Tested circulation account. Recorded interventions are compared with the circuit's predictions. Agreement strengthens this account, while the archive preserves that quantitative, experimental and analogical arguments worked together.

Connected circulation diagram. The later capillary evidence supplies an observed connection that the earlier circuit needed. The combined diagram spans different investigators and generations. Medical historian: “That much blood cannot simply be used up each minute. The circuit makes sense of the quantities; the later capillary observations connect what the earlier argument could not yet show.”

Average acceleration. A velocity change from2m/s to8m/s over3s gives average acceleration2m/s². This finite-interval result is not automatically instantaneous acceleration throughout the interval.
Difference quotient. A secant slope compares a curve's change in value with its change in input. Shrinking the interval asks whether those slopes approach a stable limit.
Derivative. Where the limit exists, the derivative describes local change. A sharp corner is a useful warning: not every drawn curve has a derivative everywhere.

Force model. Mass times the example’s average acceleration gives its average net-force requirement in the Newtonian model. It does not by itself identify which physical interaction supplies that force.
Velocity function. Differentiating the smooth position model produces its velocity function. This is a result about the fitted model, not direct differentiation of isolated raw measurements.

Orbital model. A proposed inverse-square attraction is tested against the motion requirements and recorded orbits in this idealized Newtonian case. The candidate law supplies content that 'force' alone could not.
Displacement sum. Small signed velocity×time contributions add to displacement. Traveling +6m then−4m gives net displacement2m, even though the total distance traveled is10m.

Integral. The integral is the limit of these displacement sums. To obtain total distance, integrate speed—the absolute value of velocity—instead; the distinction survives arbitrarily fine slices. Mathematics correspondent: “Forward and backward motion no longer vanish into one misleading distance. We have a way to reckon change, and an orbital model whose predictions can meet observations.”

Equiprobable outcome list. The next two fair rounds have four equally likely winner sequences: AA, AB, BA, BB. If the match finishes early, the unused round can still be listed to compare equally likely cases.
Frequency table. The frequency table records repeated outcomes, including disappointing runs. A short sequence need not resemble its long-run model closely.

Updated odds. This explicitly modern extension multiplies prior odds by a likelihood ratio. Prior odds1:4 and likelihood ratio3 give posterior odds3:4—not probability3/4, and not a result from the1654 letters.
Probability. In this equiprobable example, favorable cases divided by all cases gives a probability. A general sample space need not have equal probabilities; that assumption belongs to this game.
Empirical distribution. Relative frequencies form an empirical distribution of this record. The record can challenge an assumed model without proving exactly what will happen next.
Expected value. Weight each payout by its probability and add. Expected value describes an average under the model, not what any one play must pay.
Risk table. The risk table keeps losses beside their probabilities. Equal expected values can conceal very different worst cases and matter differently to different players.
Fair stake division. At2–1 in a first-to-three match, the leader wins unless the other player wins twice: probability3/4. Divide four coins as3 and1, not in the current-score ratio2:1.

Revised risk estimate. The revised probabilities change the risk estimate while leaving the possible losses visible. The likelihood model and prior remain contestable; a numerical update is not manufactured certainty. Letter writer: “Three coins to the leader, one to the opponent: the unfinished match is settled by its remaining possibilities. Our other estimate can change when evidence does—not when certainty is demanded.”

Clock movement. The oscillator supplies a repeated motion and the escapement meters the clock's movement. A regular tick on land is only the beginning of the navigation problem.

Time difference. At the instant of local noon, this idealized example's reference clock reads14:00. The simultaneous difference is two hours; comparing readings from different moments would be meaningless.

Reference sky time. The corrected Moon–star observation is compared with lunar tables to estimate reference time. This idealized card assumes necessary observational corrections; it is not a complete navigation procedure.
Compensated clock. Temperature compensation aims to reduce changes in timekeeping as conditions vary. The design must be tested; attaching the name 'compensation' does not establish its accuracy.

Longitude estimate. Earth turns15degrees per hour, so that two-hour difference corresponds to30degrees. With the reference clock ahead at local noon, this idealized position is west of the reference meridian.
Lunar-distance fix. Reference sky time is compared with the ship's local astronomical time at that same observation. Local noon from another moment is not a substitute.
Marine timekeeper. The mounting is intended to keep time through ship motion. Sea conditions ask a different question from a quiet workshop demonstration.
Placed.
Tested chronometer. The trial log records how the timekeeper performed at sea. One good voyage still leaves durability, cost and repeatable manufacture open to examination.
Chronometer fix. The tested timekeeper supports this clock-based fix, with its accumulated error carried forward. A reliable instrument and a correct calculation are distinct requirements.

Cross-checked position. In the fictional trial, clock and lunar fixes differ by2degrees. The disagreement triggers checking errors before approaching a coast; averaging them blindly could preserve a shared mistake. Navigation examiner: “The two fixes disagree by two degrees. That warning belongs in the voyage record: the next crew needs our checks and doubts, not a reassuring average.”

Sedimentary sequence. The lower and upper beds record separate episodes of sediment accumulation. Their order is evidence; the section does not supply a calendar date by itself.
Deformation record. The older beds are now steeply tilted. Their present orientation records deformation after deposition rather than proving sediment originally fell vertically.
Erosion interval. The tilted beds are truncated at a surface. Material is missing: erosion can leave a boundary that is positive evidence of an intervening event.
Unconformity. Younger beds lie across the eroded older beds at a different angle. The angular unconformity requires more than one uninterrupted episode of deposition.
Stratigraphic section. The labeled section keeps the crossing relationships visible: deposition, deformation, erosion, then renewed deposition. A drawing makes the proposed event order checkable.
Relative chronology. The crossing relationships constrain a relative chronology. They establish before and after without assigning an unsupported number of years.
Correlated strata. A later comparison introduces William Smith's use of characteristic fossil assemblages to recognize strata. This is not attributed to Hutton's1788 visit.
Deep-time argument. Repeated ordinary processes require substantial time in Hutton's account. Siccar Point supports that reasoning; it did not create the whole theory in a single instant.

Regional sequence. Comparing fossil-bearing sections can connect layers across a region even where surface appearance differs. Smith's1815 mapping is the historical case; any particular match still needs evidence.

Geological history. The account distinguishes Hutton's event sequence from the later fossil-mapping comparison. The atlas now explains both missing time in one section and correlations between sections. Field geologist: “The missing years are part of the record too. Our section shows what happened before what; the later fossil comparisons help us connect it to other outcrops.”

Variable population. The recorded population contains differences among individuals. Treating every specimen as an imperfect copy of one ideal would discard the variation the explanation needs.
Relationship hypothesis. Shared characters suggest a relationship hypothesis. Similarity can also arise independently, so resemblance alone is not an infallible family tree.
Isolation hypothesis. A geographic barrier can reduce exchange between populations. It proposes a mechanism for divergence, but isolation alone does not determine the eventual outcome.
Heritable variation. Some recorded differences recur across generations in the teaching case. Heritability, not merely visible difference, is needed for this selection model.
Branching descent. The branching diagram represents divergence, not a ladder with humans at its summit. Living branches have their own histories rather than being unfinished ancestors of one another.
Selection model. Individuals with a heritable difference leave different numbers of descendants under these conditions. That can change a population without any individual deciding to evolve.
Biogeographic account. The island distribution is compared with a branching account and barriers. Geography becomes evidence about relationships rather than decoration around a list of species.
Historical descent evidence. The fossil sequence tests whether the proposed history fits earlier forms. Incomplete preservation limits what absence can establish.
Adaptation model. A trait helpful in one environment can be costly in another. Adaptation here is a context-dependent fit, not movement toward a universal best organism.

Evolutionary explanation. The explanation joins branching history with a possible mechanism of change. Darwin and Wallace are contributors to this case, not licenses to turn biological selection into a moral rule. Natural-history correspondent: “The islands belong in the explanation, not merely on the map. We can now compare a branching history with the specimens, without making every branch a rung toward perfection.”

Case map. The marks locate recorded deaths; Snow’s historical map used bars. A dense cluster can reflect exposure, population density or reporting, so a map is a question-generating tool rather than a verdict.
Mortality rates. Deaths are compared with households served. A supplier with more deaths but many more customers need not have the higher rate.
Supplier comparison. Rates are grouped by water supplier rather than just by street. The comparison now addresses a possible exposure difference.
Exposure history. A witness reports using a different water source from the one expected at the address. Interview evidence exposes a possible classification error in the neat map.
Natural-experiment comparison. Intermingled households help compare suppliers within shared neighborhoods. This was not random assignment; remaining household differences still deserve investigation.
Exposure classification. Receipts and supplier records are checked against the household account. Exposure must be established, not guessed solely from geographic proximity.
Exposure-risk estimate. The revised exposure groups change the calculated risk comparison. A quantitative result depends on how cases and denominators were classified.
Converging evidence. The map, interviews and rate comparison address related parts of the same question. They overlap in data and are not automatically independent confirmations.
Causal assessment. Alternative explanations are weighed against the exposure evidence. This supports a causal assessment while retaining observational limitations.

Water-safety recommendation. A water-safety intervention can be recommended without pretending every causal uncertainty disappeared. The archive does not claim that removing one pump handle alone ended the outbreak. Public-health archivist: “We have grounds to recommend safer water, even while questions remain. Keep the household comparison beside the recommendation so others can challenge it.”

Latent paper image. The light-sensitive paper records exposure before a clearly visible image appears. This historical-process model describes an effect, not a chemical preparation recipe.
Visible paper negative. Development makes the paper negative visible. Light and dark are reversed, which will matter when another image is made from it.
Stable negative. Fixing makes the negative sufficiently stable for the historical workflow. Preservation still depends on materials and conditions; 'stable' does not mean eternal.
Positive print. Contact printing from the negative produces a positive image. One preserved negative makes repeat copies possible, unlike a unique direct-positive object.
Print edition. Several prints can be made from the negative and compared by different viewers. Reproducibility changes who can inspect an image, not whether every interpretation is correct.
Measured photograph. A scale marker gives the photograph a reference for size in its plane. Perspective and camera position still limit measurements elsewhere in the scene.
Photographic record. Images taken at recorded times reveal change that a single photograph cannot. Differences in lighting or camera position can also masquerade as change.

Annotated visual archive. Context records explain when, where and why the images were made. A photograph can be evidence without being an interpretation-free window onto the past. Photographic archivist: “Others can now inspect prints of the same image. Keep our notes beside them: a camera records a view, not everything that happened beyond its frame.”

Carved edition. The fictional workshop carves the selected edition into a block. Its text and image can be retained together for later runs; revising that surface has a cost.
Typeset edition. Reusable pieces of type are assembled for the same edition. Setting and storing a character inventory is work, not an automatically superior replacement for carving.
Woodblock print. Paper and ink take an impression from the prepared block. The result shows that a sophisticated printed page does not require movable type.
Type print. The type produces another printed page. Similar visible results can hide very different preparation and revision workflows.
Stored-block advantage. For this unchanged reprint order, a preserved block avoids resetting the page. This local advantage does not prove block printing is always cheaper.
Reset-type advantage. For this revised order, reusable type can be rearranged instead of recarving a whole page. The advantage depends on the revision, available type and workshop labor.
Workflow comparison. The two orders favor different workflows. Their coexistence challenges the simple story that one invention must immediately make the other obsolete.

Contextual adoption account. Patrons, editions, skills and available materials help explain adoption alongside technical possibilities. This fictional comparison illustrates a historical question; it does not establish one universal cause for East Asian printing choices. Printer: “The unchanged book and the revised edition favor different tools. We will keep both workflows; an invention need not make every older practice useless.”

We retrieve our experimental protocol from the archive and enter a gallery of recorded demonstrations and enclosed educational apparatus. Other collections stay where we left them. We collect the things needed for this scene along the way.

Current-deflection record. The compass changes direction when current flows in the nearby wire. The needle is not wired into the circuit: the observation links electric current with a magnetic effect.

Magnetic-direction map. Compass directions at several positions trace a curved pattern around the bar magnet. The arrows represent local direction; they are not visible threads or a measured map of strength.

Moving-and-still record. In the supplied coil trials the needle deflects while the magnet approaches, returns to zero when it rests, and deflects the other way as it withdraws. A magnet present beside the coil is not enough for a sustained reading.

Ring transient record. The second winding gives a brief response at connection and disconnection, not a sustained response while the first current stays steady. Neither winding has to move. Faraday’s surviving 1831 ring anchors this reconstructed comparison.
Around-the-wire comparison. The recorded needles above and below the same wire point in opposite directions. A simple pull straight toward the wire does not describe this pattern.

Repeatable induction comparison. The protocol preserves the same coil, magnet orientation and meter while distinguishing approach, rest and withdrawal. Repeated recorded trials retain the zero reading at rest rather than discarding it as an uninteresting failure.

Field comparison sheet. The magnet and the current-carrying wire both organize compass directions in the space around them, but the patterns differ. Field thinking records what a test needle does at each position, rather than merely naming an attraction.

Change-not-presence argument. The moving magnet and the stationary ring support the same distinction: changing magnetic linkage, not mere magnetic presence, induces the response. Mechanical motion is one way to obtain the change, not a requirement in every arrangement.

Field-and-induction model. The model connects a spatial magnetic pattern to a changing linkage through a coil. It explains the contrasting observations without claiming that the compass map alone proves induction, or that one diagram supplies a complete electromagnetic theory.

Explained generator exhibit. The handle keeps changing magnetic linkage through the generator’s coil, and the recorded lamp responds while it turns. The handle supplies mechanical energy: the magnet is not a fuel. The exhibit now connects an everyday generator with the earlier contrast between steady presence and change. Electricity-gallery curator: “The quiet needle mattered too. Our exhibit shows why change produces a response, and why the lamp needs the work of the turning handle—not a magnet that supplies endless energy.”

We leave the explained generator in its gallery and enter a two-desk communications exhibit. Here the question is not how to power a signal, but whether the receiver can recover what the sender meant to send. We collect the things needed for this scene along the way.
Shared door-status code. Both desks now use 0 for “door closed” and 1 for “door open.” The timing convention is already shared; this agreement does not check the door itself.
Unprotected bit 0. The keeper’s report is represented by 0, ready at the sender. One unprotected bit gives the receiver no way to distinguish a valid 1 from a flipped 0.
Protected packet 000. At the sender, the original 0 becomes 000. These three copies are now ready to go through the channel; the extra two bits are a real transmission cost.
Received packet 010. The sender transmitted 000; the recorded channel delivered 010. The receiver sees a disagreement between the three copies, not three new source bits.
Recovered report: door closed. Majority decoding maps the received 010 to 0: two copies say 0. The other desk recovers the keeper’s “door closed” report without consulting the sender’s original.

Shared prefix-code table. Use 00 → 0, 01 → 10, 10 → 110, 11 → 111. No codeword begins another, so 010110111 parses as 0 | 10 | 110 | 111 and restores 00 | 01 | 10 | 11. Both desks share this new block table.

15-bit packed dispatch. The supplied batch uses 7 × 1 + 1 × 2 + 1 × 3 + 1 × 3 = 15 bits, not 20. The model’s expected length is 1.5 bits per pair: a 25% average reduction before protection. Two rare pairs expand to three bits each.

45-bit protected dispatch plan. Compress this batch to 15 bits, then triple each bit: 45 channel bits fit the window; tripling the original 20 bits would cost 60. At the receiver, majority-decode aligned triples first, then parse the prefix code. This is a costed plan for the separate batch, not a claim it has already been transmitted. Communications engineer: “The other desk recovered ‘door closed’ from 010, and the batch can be protected within 45 bits instead of 60. The link has done its job; checking the keeper’s claim is a different job. We can leave this exhibit here.”

Error bars. Repeated readings vary around an estimate. The error bars state the chosen uncertainty summary; their meaning must be named rather than inferred from their appearance.
Model comparison. Two models make different predictions for a new observation. A comparison becomes informative when evidence could favor one over the other.
Registered protocol. A timestamped protocol distinguishes planned analyses from later exploration. Exploration remains valuable, but it should not be relabeled as an earlier prediction.
Precision estimate. More observations can sharpen an estimate under the stated sampling model. Repeating a biased procedure more often does not remove its bias.
Predictive test. The new observation is compared with predictions written beforehand. A model modified after seeing the result has not passed the same test.
Replication protocol. An independent team receives enough detail to attempt the study. Independence is not sameness: differences in setting may reveal limits to the original claim.
Uncertainty statement. The uncertainty statement records sampling assumptions as well as a number. Precision about the wrong population can still mislead.
Out-of-sample assessment. Held-out observations test performance beyond the fitted examples. Repeatedly choosing models on the held-out set eventually compromises that separation.
Interpretable replication. The replication reports its uncertainty, allowing disagreement to be interpreted rather than reduced to a pass/fail slogan. A noisy replication may be inconclusive.

Robustness report. The report compares replication and held-out performance. Agreement is informative; unexplained disagreement becomes part of the record instead of disappearing into a success badge. Research editor: “The result now travels with its uncertainty and the attempts to repeat it. If the findings disagree, that disagreement stays in the record instead of being edited out.”

User-resource map. The map identifies upstream and downstream canal users, including people whose needs were absent from the official list. A resource boundary and a social boundary need not coincide.
Allocation problem. Dry-season demand exceeds the water available in the fictional case. Naming the shortage prevents a rule from promising every user everything.
Allocation rule. Users propose a timed allocation rule. It is a candidate agreement shaped by local needs, not a universal optimum supplied by the game.
Monitoring agreement. Observable flows and turns make compliance discussable. Monitoring can still be costly or uneven, so a measurable rule is not automatically a fair one.
Accountable procedure. A user can contest a recorded violation through an accessible appeal. Accountability changes who can challenge enforcement; it does not guarantee every appeal succeeds.
Revisable charter. The charter specifies how users can revise the rule after a dry season. A durable institution can include a way to change rather than pretending initial foresight was perfect.

Nested agreement. Neighboring authorities coordinate across boundaries that one canal group cannot govern alone. Ostrom's work motivates contextual, nested arrangements, not the claim that commons always beat states or markets. The water-users’ secretary folds the agreement. “The missing users are named, turns can be checked, and decisions can be challenged. I’ll bring that appeal route to the next teaching case—where a prediction may overlook us too.”

Trained predictor. The fictional predictor learns water-demand patterns from selected canal records. Cases absent from that collection may be poorly served; learning a pattern does not make every need visible.

Validation result. The earlier held-out assessment supplies a method, not a dataset: this fictional predictor is checked on canal cases withheld from fitting. Its overall score looks good, but that result need not hold for every user or setting.

Generalization assessment. The intended canal service includes downstream turns poorly represented in the fitting records. Comparing these cases with the validation result shows why a good overall score is not enough.

Disaggregated evaluation. The canal’s downstream users have more missed demand than the overall score reveals. Keeping their errors separate makes the overlooked needs discussable; it does not decide a fair allocation by itself.

Model card. The card names the fictional canal predictor’s intended use, its evaluation and its downstream limits. Users can inspect the claims; a written card does not certify that the service is fair.

Contestable decision process. The water-users’ secretary brings the appeal route from the canal agreement. A user can now challenge a prediction’s evidence or application instead of treating the score as an unanswerable judgment.

Audited service. In the canal teaching case, outcomes and appeals remain open to review after deployment. New harms or changed conditions can call for restriction or withdrawal. The inherited appeal remains useful without promising every appeal will succeed. The secretary recognizes the appeal route. “A prediction no longer ends the conversation.” The service records its limits and keeps outcomes and challenges under review; changed conditions may still call for restriction or withdrawal.

Competing reconstructions. In this fiction, two former residents remember incompatible eviction scenes; the dated street photograph constrains both but settles neither. The reconstruction now has alternatives instead of a single authoritative past.

Evidence-gap map. The only private witness to the decisive disputed act withdraws testimony, while a public court record survives; the other resident’s account of that act is indirect. The map marks what remains supported and what cannot be reconstructed from admissible material.

Walkable neighborhood. The fictional spatial engine lets visitors walk the competing neighborhood models. The new power is vivid access to lost places; vividness can also make an uncertain account feel indisputably real.
Uncertainty overlay. An overlay ties disputed parts of each scene to their sources and gaps. Visitors can see uncertainty rather than mistake a smooth rendering for complete knowledge.
Disputed restitution. An ownership claimant uses the reconstructed scene to seek restitution. A compelling simulation now affects present rights, even though its evidential gaps have not vanished.

Qualified reconstruction. The walkable reconstruction keeps those uncertainty marks visible. It gains honesty at the cost of a seamless illusion; the missing testimony is not magically recovered by consent software.

Contested case file. The hearing records conflicting claims and reasons without making the player pronounce a final legal verdict. Procedural access does not erase unequal resources between claimants.

Open restitution case. The restitution case remains open beside a qualified reconstruction. Descendants gain a way to contest erasure, but the archive cannot manufacture the unknowable event that would settle every claim. Archive steward: “We can walk these streets again without concealing the gaps in their testimony. The eviction claim remains open; a vivid reconstruction cannot supply the missing witness.”

Extended-light forecast. In the fictional model, a mirror schedule adds light during part of the growing season. Extra light is only a proposed benefit: crops also depend on heat, water and biological responses.
Lost observing window. The schedule overlaps a neighboring observatory's dark-time window. The same reflected light is a resource for one group and lost observing capacity for another.
Conditional harvest forecast. The water budget limits the modeled harvest gain. A brighter field is not automatically a larger sustainable harvest, and the forecast is explicitly conditional.
Darkness-impact map. The habitat record expands the dispute beyond people and telescopes. Darkness has ecological roles that a simple crop-yield total would leave out.
Lower-light plan. An alternative orbit reduces the illumination and the predicted crop benefit. This is a concrete compromise, not a discovery of a free solution that satisfies everyone.

Shared-sky proposal. The proposal displays harvest limits beside observing and habitat losses. Different communities can reasonably weigh those outcomes differently; the artifact makes the disagreement legible.
Stoppable pilot. The fictional shutter can halt further illumination. Stoppable operation is a technical control, not proof that earlier ecological or social effects can be reversed.
Irreversible-risk record. The record separates what stops immediately from changes that may persist. It rejects the tempting equation 'off switch equals no lasting harm.'

Living atlas of consequences. The keeper receives an atlas representing the memory dispute and the shared-sky dispute, with supported claims, competing interests and unanswered questions. Its next reader can inspect and challenge the account. The commission is complete; restitution and the consequences of the mirror remain open. The archive keeper closes the atlas, leaving room for corrections. “The lost neighborhood and the shared night sky are both here, with the claims we could support and the questions we could not settle. It is ready for its next reader—not because our answers are final, but because someone else can examine them.”
